newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-China doctor raises heights and also hopes.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-China doctor raises heights and also hopes.

text.p: Chinese people who pay a visit to Dr Xia Hetao may walk away literally feeling a little taller.
From his tidy office at the Capital University of Medical Sciences in southwestern Beijing, Xia runs the Institute of External Skeletal Fixation Technology. In plainer language, he stretches bones.

Xia has used his bone-growing methods -- which he learned from Soviet physicians in the 1980s -- to help hundreds of people with deformed or abnormally short limbs, but also to give some vertically challenged Chinese a leg up on life.
"There is a vast difference in the physiques of people in our country, and the proportion of short people is relatively large," Xia told Reuters in an interview.
Most patients add just a few cm (about one inch) but Xia has succeeded in making a leg grow by as much as 16.5 cm (6.5 inches).
SURGERY COSTS AN ARM AND A LEG
The procedure is not for the faint of heart.

The bone of an arm, leg or finger is cut in two and a steel frame fitted around the body part to provide support. The trick is to keep the two sections of bone slightly apart, forcing new bone to grow in and fill the gap.

The patient must daily crank the halves farther apart so the bone continually grows until the desired length is reached. A high-calcium diet is necessary to promote bone growth and a long physical therapy period is needed to build up the muscles and let the skin regenerate.

Despite its grisliness, people fork out an arm and a leg for the surgery, which costs from 20-30,000 yuan ($2,400-$3,600), compared with an average monthly salary of 446 yuan for a Chinese urban resident.
PROCEDURE HAS UPS AND DOWNS

Xia says his institute offers the most advanced and safest techniques and he has a bone to pick with doctors in other parts of China who attempt the procedure without having mastered all its complexities.
"One patient in the end was unable to walk and there was another one who had to have his legs amputated after the procedure," he said.
Successful surgery has helped many people with deformities to live a more normal life in a society where the disabled are often treated as inferiors or freaks, he said.
"If the technique has been mastered, it can be a blessing to people, but if you haven't mastered it completely, it can be disastrous," he said.
Xia said more people who are perfectly healthy but who feel they are too short have been asking about the procedure, hoping a boost in physical stature will also boost their social standing.
"Some people have difficulty finding work because they are too short," he said.
"Concerning finding a marriage partner or falling in love, I have received many letters from people saying because they were born short they suffered and are looking for some solace," he said.
LEGAL WORRIES TO CUT DOWN BUSINESS

Xia said he is uneasy carrying out the technique on healthy people but readily talks about one 1.75-metre (5 foot 9 inch) woman who underwent the unpleasant procedure to add three cm so she could qualify for modelling school.
"She wanted it to be done faster, within 40 days, because she had a show coming up," he said.
Fearing that doing the procedure on those who aren't really in need may create legal problems if something goes awry, Xia is trying to cut down on the number of people looking for a lift up.
Xia has set guidelines saying women should be under 1.40 metres (4 feet 7 inches) while men have to come in at under 1.60 metres (5 feet 3 inches).
Under those standards, China's late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who died last February, would have qualified. He stood at just 1.50 metres (4 feet 11 inches).
